newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finland still sees no need to join NATO -- President.
newsitem.headline: Finland still sees no need to join NATO -- President.

text.p: Finland, a European Union newcomer which shares a long border with Russia, is relaxed about remaining outside NATO, President Martti Ahtisaari said on Monday.
Ahtisaari, Finland's first directly elected president, said it was outdated to suggest fear of its giant eastern neighbour may be holding back a NATO application.

"I wish more people would visit this country and recognise that despite the fact that we have a 1,300 km border with Russia ... we are not losing a good night's sleep over that," he told Reuters in an interview.

Encouraged after the 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union, once-isolated Finland has moved toward integration with Europe, but Ahtisaari made clear Helsinki is not joining a current scramble to enter NATO.

The Western alliance plans to admit several East European countries, likely to be decided next year. The 16-member North Atlantic Treaty Organisation is conferring with Russia to allay its fears about this eastward expansion.
Ahtisaari, who took office a year before the country joined the EU in 1995, said it was anachronistic to ask if Finland, which maintains a non-aligned stance, dared seek to join NATO.
"The one who asks that sort of question is saying -- I think the person is living in the Cold War," he said. "It's a totally wrong way of putting it."
EU membership was long ruled out because of Finland's policy of neutrality but the Soviet collapse inccreased the country's room for manoeuvre.
Finland was twice at war against the Soviet Union in 1939-1944 after which it ceded about one tenth of its territory but held on to its independence.

The constitutional head of Finland's foreign policy, Ahtisaari was speaking in the wake of several visits by leaders of the Western alliance to Finland, and said he welcomed a current debate here about possible membership.

But for Finland -- which participates in NATO's Partnership for Peace Programme designed to bring together forces across the former Cold War divide -- he said security now derives from a complex combination of allegiances and cooperation.

"Now and in the near future it's clearly so that we are making our best contribution to our own security and European security by not applying for membership," he said. "But that doesn't prevent us from having cooperation."
Discussing Finland's evolution since the breakup of the Soviet Union, formerly a major trading partner, Ahtisaari said: "We perhaps came out of the Cold War period much faster than many others."

"We Finns are extremely realistic," he said. "You should ask yourself ... the same question that we ask ourselves: would (NATO membership) increase our security ... whether this would help European security," he said.
For now, the clear consensus, both among Finns and those he met at a diplomatic level, was that it would not.
"Of course in theory the option is there -- (but) we didn't join the Partnership for Peace as an ante-chamber for membership," he said.

International organisations were changing and would change even more next year, he said, but the idea of a Finnish NATO application was so distant that there had not even been any discussion of the procedure on how Finland would decide.
"It's even more remote than my second term," he said, referring to questions recently raised in Finnish media about whether he would run again when his term expires in 2000.
